documents.title: International standards for neurological classification of spinal cord injury revised

chunks.content: Administrative information Note: The numbers in curly brackets in this protocol refer to SPIRIT checklist item numbers. The order of the items has been modified to group similar items (see http://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/spirit-2013-statement-defining-standard-protocol-items-for-clinical-trials/ ). Background Background and rationale {6a} Spinal cord damage disrupts nerve connections between the brain and the body’s ascending sensory and descending motor pathways. The spinal cord, part of the central nervous system, transports nerve signals in and out of the brain and cooperates with peripheral nerves to enable voluntary and involuntary motor activity, sensory perception, and environmental interaction. The nerve connection is incomplete or completely disrupted when a spinal cord injury occurs. In the former, sub-lesional sensations and movements persist, whereas in the latter all function is lost and paralysis develops [ ]. The phases of spinal cord injury are divided into five phases as follows: (1) Early acute phase (first 2 to 48 h), (2) acute phase (first 2 h to 2 weeks), (3) subacute phase (day 2 to end of the week 2), (4) intermediate phase (week 2 to month 6), and (5) chronic phase (month 6 to onwards) [ ]. Globally, 20·6 million individuals experienced SCI in 2019. The incidence and prevalence of spinal injuries in China have increased by 98.20%, respectively, the most significant increase among G20 countries [ ]. Most traumatic SCIs in 1999 were caused by falls (52.4%). At 26.4%, traffic accidents were the second most common cause. Traffic accidents cause the most SCIs, followed by falls [ ]. SCI can be classified as a complete or incomplete injury based on severity. Incomplete SCI can present as central core syndrome, Brown-Séquard syndrome, anterior cord syndrome, or posterior core syndrome [ ]. Based on the International Standards for Neurological Classification and the American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS), spinal cord injuries are categorized as either complete or incomplete. Complete injuries are classified as AIS-A, whereas incomplete injuries are classified as AIS-B, AIS-C, AIS-D, or AIS-E, depending on the extent of motor and sensory impairment. A person’s injury is considered complete if they lack voluntary anal contraction, which is indicative of a motor lesion in the S4/5 region, as well as sensation surrounding the anus, which is indicative of a sensory lesion in the S4/5 region [ ]. Paralysis is the primary and evident outcome of spinal cord injury (SCI), resulting in patients experiencing either partial or complete lack of sensation and movement [ ]. Human gait requires lower extremity muscle force, joint proprioception, visual balance, and cognition. Joint proprioception and visual function can also impact balance ability. Following a spinal cord injury (SCI), individuals encounter a range of proprioceptive deficits. It is crucial for rehabilitating movement and acquiring new abilities after spinal cord injury (SCI) [ ]. ASIA/IMSOP, the international standard for spinal cord trauma neurological assessment, is the most accurate and closest to standardization. The WISCI improves walking levels more accurately than the FIM, although the FIM measures patient self-care and independence better [ ]. SCI-related changes in muscle function are often examined via electromyography (EMG). Paralyzed muscles exhibit aberrant neuromuscular transmission, motor unit recruitment and discharge patterns, loss of functioning motor units, and structural reorganization, according to electromyography (EMG) analysis [ ]. Clinical outcomes with neurorehabilitation robots are promising. Robot-assisted gait training improves neuroplasticity, which helps injured nerves recover through repetitive training and stimulation. Second, this training can increase a patient’s muscle strength, stability, walking efficiency, and safety [ ]. Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) is a noninvasive neuromodulation method. This technology may help us understand spinal interneuronal activity and improve rehabilitation for neurological illnesses, including spinal cord injury [ ]. The gold standard for SCI rehabilitation is repetitive motor activity, commonly employed in clinics to help patients recover. Exercise after SCI appears to excite the neural system enough to activate undamaged spinal pathways and residual supraspinal inputs [ ]. The combination of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) with robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) is an area of growing interest. Some research suggests that including tSCS may improve the effects of robotic training on balance and movement; however, specific investigations on this combination in SCI patients are still limited [ , ]. Most existing research has focused on the efficacy of tSCS or RAGT alone, leaving a gap in understanding the potential synergistic effects of these therapies when used together. There is also a lack of reliable biomarkers for functional recovery, with intramuscular electromyography (iEMG) showing promise in other neurological conditions but underexplored in SCI patients undergoing tSCS and RAGT. Although there has been much research on RAGT, this study makes a unique contribution by looking at the combined impacts of RAGT and tSCS. This combination could have synergistic benefits, especially regarding walking speed, endurance, and overall gait quality. Furthermore, this trial is the only one that keeps both groups receiving

tSCS or RAGT alone, leaving a gap in understanding the potential synergistic effects of these therapies when used together. There is also a lack of reliable biomarkers for functional recovery, with intramuscular electromyography (iEMG) showing promise in other neurological conditions but underexplored in SCI patients undergoing tSCS and RAGT. Although there has been much research on RAGT, this study makes a unique contribution by looking at the combined impacts of RAGT and tSCS. This combination could have synergistic benefits, especially regarding walking speed, endurance, and overall gait quality. Furthermore, this trial is the only one that keeps both groups receiving transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS). Compared to conventional methodologies, this approach offers new insights into the effectiveness of robotic training by isolating its impact on gait progress. Our findings may greatly aid our understanding of how combining tSCS and RAGT may improve rehabilitation outcomes may be significantly aided by our findings. Furthermore, our research aligns with existing clinical procedures, which frequently combine gait therapy with tSCS. As a biomarker, intramuscular EMG could provide valuable insights into neuromuscular changes during and after rehabilitation, helping tailor rehabilitation programs to individual needs and track progress more accurately. Standardization and protocol development can improve consistency and comparability of future studies, facilitating the development of evidence-based guidelines for clinical practice. Studying the long-term effects of combined tSCS and RAGT can provide evidence of the sustainability of functional improvements, which is crucial for clinical decision-making. Understanding these therapies’ mechanisms can lead to optimized treatment strategies and potentially uncover new therapeutic targets. Objectives {7} This study aimed to determine the effects of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation combined with robot-assisted gait training for improving balance and mobility in patients with incomplete spinal cord injury (intermediate phase). Consequently, the research questions of this investigation are as follows: What are the impacts of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation combined with robot-assisted gait training for improving balance and mobility in patients with spinal cord injury? We hypothesized that (1) combined training will result in more significant changes leading to more substantial enhancements in the functional capacity of balance and mobility in people with SCI. Therefore, the objectives of this study are to (1) examine the effects of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation combined with robot-assisted gait training for improving balance and mobility in people with SCI and (2) provide evidence to clarify the mechanisms by which balance and mobility function recover in people with SCI. Trial design {8} This is a prospective, double-blind, parallel-armed randomized controlled trial. The 20 selected subjects with SCI were divided into two groups: A and B. Group A comprised 13 subjects, and Group B comprised 7 subjects. Group A (the experimental group) received robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) + transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS), and Group B (the control group) received conventional physical therapy (CPT) + transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) for 8 weeks, 5 sessions a week. Figure shows the flow chart of the trial process. The checklist of Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) is provided in Additional File 1: Table S1. Methods Study setting {9} The study setting was Xi'an International Medical Center Hospital. Eligibility criteria {10} The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Both male and female subjects who were diagnosed with incomplete spinal cord injury (SCI) and (2) who were rated with an AIS score of B, C, or D on the American Spinal Cord Injury Association Impairment Scale (ASIA scale). (3) Eligible participants must be between 18 and 80 and (4) at least 3 months post-injury (intermediate phase, week 2 to month 6). The exclusion criteria for the study included the following: (1) Having a cardiac pacemaker, (2) having unstable angina or other decompensated heart disease, (3) having a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or dysreflexia of the autonomic system; (4) individuals with a tracheostomy, (5) significant deformity, or stiffness in the hip joint, knee (20° or more of flexion), or ankle (10° or more of plantar flexion) and those with a restricted range of motion are excluded; (6) additional exclusions apply to those lacking cardiovascular conditioning or disabling fatigue; (7) a body weight greater than 135 kg, a body height greater than 2 m, and a leg length difference greater than 2 cm; (9) osteoporosis; and (10) unstable fractures in the lower extremity or decubitus ulcers on the back or lower extremities. Who will take informed consent? {26a} Potential trial participants were provided with an explanation of the trial by professional rehabilitation therapists. The therapists acquired the participants’ signatures on the informed consent form who showed willingness to participate in the trial. Additional consent provisions for the collection and use of participant data and biological specimens {26b} N/A. Interventions Explanation for the choice of comparators {6b} Clinical outcomes with neurorehabilitation robots are promising. Robot-assisted gait training improves neuroplasticity, which helps injured nerves recover through repetitive training and stimulation. Second, this training can increase a patient’s muscle strength, stability, walking efficiency, and safety. Electrodes on the skin stimulate spinal circuitries via electrical current in transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS), a noninvasive neuromodulation method. This technology may help us understand spinal interneuronal activity and improve rehabilitation for neurological illnesses, including spinal cord injury. The gold standard for SCI rehabilitation is repetitive motor activity, commonly employed in clinics to help patients recover. Exercise after SCI appears to excite the neural system enough to activate undamaged spinal pathways and residual supraspinal inputs [ – ]. Intervention description {11a} The training program for both groups was constructed using the study intervention description from the TIDieR template. Specific information can be found in Additional File 2: Table S2. Each group was undergoing training consisting of 30 30-min sessions per week for 8 weeks. A single instructor with a physical therapy background oversees each training session. The ratio of instructors to participants was 1:1. The training sessions were conducted exclusively in a designated rehabilitation room within the hospital premises. The training sessions for the two groups are scheduled at separate times of the day to ensure that participants are not subjected to additional interventions. Throughout the workout, the participants were closely observed and supervised to ensure their safety and prevent any falls or injuries associated with falling. <italic toggle="yes">Robot-assisted gait training (RAGT)</italic> + <italic toggle="yes">transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS)</italic> The patient received 40 sessions, 5 sessions per week for 8 weeks, of 30 min (Novo Skeleton AVIC Trands Robot Xi'an Co., Ltd., China), and 20 min of tSCS was applied at the beginning of each session. During Novo Skeleton training, the patient fits with a harness and unloads 50% of his body weight. The parameters are adjusted according to the physical characteristics of the patient. The training speed varies between 1.0 and 1.5 km/h, being slow at the beginning of the session and progressively increasing while maintaining gait quality. tSCS was delivered via self-adhesive body surface electrodes for physical therapy BC4060R (pin type); the cathode electrode (4 cm × 6 cm) was placed over (not on the bone but specifically over the soft tissue parallel to the spine) the T11–T12 intervertebral space, and two interconnected reference electrodes (anode) (4 cm × 6 cm) were placed symmetrically at both sides of the umbilicus. A biphasic square current was applied via an electro-stimulator (Xiangyu Electrode Sheet Model 2.0 aperture (TENS), Xiangyu Medical China) with a frequency of 30 Hz and a pulse duration of 1 ms. The stimulation intensity was used at the maximum intensity the patient tolerates during walking because it enhances muscle activation. During volitional exercise, robot-assisted gait training and maximum intensity of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation can significantly increase functional ambulation and independence. For those with spinal cord injuries (SCI), high-intensity electrical stimulation can be quite helpful when it comes to volitional exercises. A pulse that lasts at least 200 µs, with a frequency of 20–60 Hz and an amplitude of up to 300 mA, is recommended because it can help induce powerful muscular contractions and enhance functional mobility. Denervated muscles, which may need up to 100 times more energy to contract, respond best to higher intensities. This stimulation supports the rehabilitative process by promoting cardiovascular health, reducing spasticity, and facilitating muscular strengthening [ , ]. <italic toggle="yes">Conventional physical therapy (CPT)</italic> + <italic toggle="yes">transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS)</italic> Twenty minutes of tSCS was applied at the beginning of each session. Criteria for discontinuing or modifying allocated interventions {11b} Participants will be terminated from the trial if they exhibit irreversible exercise-related adverse events, including nausea, dizziness, disorientation, postural instability, and fatigue, even if the trial is exceedingly secure. Strategies to improve adherence to interventions {11c} To optimize instruction compliance, we implement the following strategies: A rigorous training plan was established for each subject every week during the 40-day training period, and the participants’ current circumstances were adjusting the schedule. The feedback and endurance of the participants were closely monitored during the training process. The intervention’s impact on the subjects during training was assessed daily. The decision of patients to withdraw from the study was facilitated. Relevant concomitant care permitted or prohibited during the trial {11d} There are no restrictions regarding concomitant care during the trial. Firstly, no concomitant care participants have been enrolled in the trial due to prior exclusions. There are currently no participants receiving concomitant care. Consequently, there have been no reported complications related to concomitant care. Secondly, concomitant care is not expressly prohibited throughout the trial. However, it is essential to consider the possible interactions and effects that other drugs or treatments may have on the primary and secondary endpoints of the research. We have put the following strategies into practice to lessen any possible confusing factors: Informed consent Participants were asked to disclose any new drugs or treatments they plan to start during the trial, and they were fully educated about the possible risks and benefits of concurrent care. Data collection Including dosage, duration, and reasons for use, we gathered comprehensive information on all concurrent drugs and treatments. Statistical analysis To identify any confounding effects, our statistical analysis plan incorporated techniques to evaluate the possible influence of concurrent care on the study’s outcomes. Through meticulous evaluation and resolution of these variables, our goal is to guarantee the experiment’s validity and the dependability of the results. Provisions for posttrial care {30} N/A. The current study design does not consider ancillary or posttrial care provisions. Additionally, participants will not be harmed by participating in the trial; thus, remuneration for their time is not expected (Tables and ). Outcomes {12} We measured all outcomes twice, once before and once after the 8 weeks of training (Table ), except demographic data. Primary outcomes Berg Balance Scale (BBS) The BBS is a scale of 14 items that measure balance and the likelihood of falling by direct observation. The items are evaluated using a range from 0 to 4, where a score of 0 indicates an inability to complete the assignment and a score of 4 signifies the successful completion of individual tasks. The calculation results in a total score of 56 possible points. The 0–20, 21–40, and 41–56 ratings signify balance impairment, acceptability, and sound, respectively. The BBS has demonstrated exceptional consistency among different raters and within the same rater, with reliability coefficients of 0.99 (95% CI, 0.97–1.00) and perfect agreement with concurrent measures, with a validity coefficient of 1.00 (95% CI, 1.00–1.00) in individuals with incomplete spinal cord damage [ ]. Timed Up and Go (TUG) test Those taking part lay back on the chair, ensuring their hips are far back and their arms are relaxed at their sides or in their laps rather than resting on the armrests. The timer starts counting down from the moment the examiner says “Go,” signaling the start of the test. Afterwards, they get up from their seats, walk 3 m, turn around, return to their seats, and then put themselves back down. The amount of time needed to finish the test determines the score [ ]. at their sides or in their laps rather than resting on the armrests. The timer starts counting down from the moment the examiner says “Go,” signaling the start of the test. Afterwards, they get up from their seats, walk 3 m, turn around, return to their seats, and then put themselves back down. The amount of time needed to finish the test determines the score [ ]. Secondary outcomes 10-m walk test (10MWT) One straightforward and often used metric of walking speed is the 10-m walk test (10MWT). Usually, spanning 10 m, it evaluates a person’s stride pace over a small distance. Ten meters (32.8 ft) of individuals walk without help; time is measured for the intermediate 6 m (19.7 feet) to enable acceleration and deceleration. They are starting time when the leading foot’s toes reach the 2-m mark. The timing is stopped when the leading foot’s toes reach the 8-m mark. Assistive tools should be kept constant and recorded from test to test. Should physical help be needed for walking, this should be done at either the preferred walking speed or the fastest speed achievable. Documentation should include the speed tested (preferred vs. fast) to collect three trials and calculate the average of the three trials. In those with SCI, the 10MWT has shown excellent concept validity (TUG: r = 0.89; 6mWT: r = 0.95) and exceptional test–retest reliability (ICC = 0.983) [ ]. Walking Index for Spinal Cord Injury (WISCI II) scale The Walking Index for Spinal Cord Injury (WISCI) is a scale used to assess the functional capacity of individuals with SCI regarding their ability to walk. It measures the degree of improvement in ambulation by evaluating the level of physical help, braces, or gadgets needed to walk 10 m. The WISCI II is the latest version. Participants are methodically advanced through a recognized sequence of capacity levels, utilizing gadgets and personal support until they reach their maximum walking ability. The WISCI II categories’ levels are based on the extent of underlying impairment rather than the requirement for physical support, walking aids, or braces. The reliability of repeated WISCI-II scores was high, as measured by intra-rater and inter-rater assessments. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for intra-rater reliability was 0.98, with a confidence interval (CI) of 0.95–0.99. The ICC for inter-rater reliability was 0.97, with a CI of 0.96–0.99 [ ]. Intramuscular electromyography (iEMG) An electrically evoked potential instrument NDI-096-C1 (Suzhou Haishen Medical Equipment Co., Ltd., China) acquired EMG signals at 10,240 Hz and bandpass filters between 100 and 4400 Hz. The intramuscular needle electrode was 0.11 mm in diameter, and a 0.002 m 2 recording area was used for disposable EN-C40 (Suzhou Haishen Medical Equipment Co., Ltd, China). These electrodes were installed with a 0.45-G needle. The fine wires were placed in muscle bellies with a 0.45-gauge hypodermic needle. Before the electrodes were inserted, chlorhexidine was used to clean the area. The electrode’s end connection was fixed after insertion, preventing tugging. The bilateral vastus lateralis (VL), bicep femoris (BF), tibialis anterior (TA), and gastrocnemius medialis capture iEMG activity. Roller bandages are placed on each volunteer’s leg to gather the system’s wire, allowing mobility and eliminating physical interference and noise. Ten ankle flexions and extensions followed 10 knee flexions and extensions. Due to their invasiveness, internal EMG electrodes are rarely utilized. This approach evaluates deep and small cross sections of muscles. Intramuscular EMG is better than surface EMG because it can detect little interference in static and dynamic muscle EMG signals. Every electrode provides a local muscle activity image [ ]. American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale According to the International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI), the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale (AIS) is the main instrument used in the evaluation of neurological outcomes following spinal cord injury (SCI) [ ]. An instrument that rates motor and sensory ability numerically and provides an alphabetical grade (A–E) to indicate the degree of disability below the level of injury [ ]. The sensory examination tests 28 dermatomes bilaterally for light touch (usually a piece of cotton) and pinprick (usually a clean safety pin). Every examination component is noted for every dermatome and laterality. The absence of sensation is indicated by a score of 0; impaired or changed sensation is indicated by a score of 1, and normal sensation is indicated by a score of 2. With 28 dermatomes, each with 2/2 points for mild touch and 2/2 points for pinprick, a normal unilateral sensory evaluation yields 112 total points. A total normal sensory assessment is a bilateral score of 224. Technically, the inability to differentiate pinprick sensation from mild touch is evaluated as 0 [ ]. Sample size {14} The sample size was calculated via the OpenEpi tool via balance as an outcome measure from the study “Effect of Robotic-assisted Gait Training on Functional and Psychological Improvement in Patients with Incomplete Spinal Cord Injury” [ ]. The level of significance (Z1-α/2) is set at 95%, with an expected mean change in the control group (µ1) of 12.9 and the experimental group (µ2) of 14.3. The anticipated standard deviation for the control group (δ1) is 0.2, whereas for the experimental group (δ2), it is 1.4. The study is powered at 80% (Z1-β) to detect a significant difference between the groups. The initial expected sample size is 18, and after accounting for a 10% dropout rate, the sample size is adjusted to 20. Consequently, the sample size for Group A (control) is 13, and that for Group B (experimental) is 7. The explanation or source for the estimated effect sizes or deviations in the power calculation was provided by referencing the study titled “Effect of Robotic-assisted Gait Training on Functional and Psychological Improvement in Patients with Incomplete Spinal Cord Injury.” The expected mean changes (1.9 for the control group and 14.3 for the experimental group) and the anticipated standard deviations (0.2 for the control group and 1.4 for the experimental group) were derived from this study. This source provides the basis for these estimates, ensuring the power calculation is grounded in empirical data relevant to the research context. The calculation also incorporates a 10% dropout rate adjustment to account for potential participant attrition, further refining the sample size estimates to ensure the study’s validity and reliability. The control group method and efficacy are already mature and effective methods in our hospital. In this experiment, it was only once again proven to be a stable therapy, and the results were also stable, without the need for more cases, which is 1/2 of the experimental group. Integrating the findings from this study with results from similar studies through meta-analysis or systematic review can provide a broader perspective and enhance the overall evidence base by aggregating data across studies, improving the generalizability of the conclusions. Additionally, performing nonparametric tests is advantageous with small samples because they require fewer assumptions, are robust to outliers, and offer more straightforward, reliable results. These tests focus on ranking or ordinal data, making them flexible and applicable to various data types, especially when parametric assumptions are not met. Recruitment {15} The participants were recruited from among the inpatients of Xi'an International Medical Center Hospital, Xi'an, China. Before recruiting volunteers, the research team conducted screenings to determine their eligibility. During the follow-up, all patients were informed of the study’s development and preliminary findings. Furthermore, the researchers were in continual communication with the treatment physicians of each patient. After the study, a final report detailing the findings was sent to the patients and the doctors. Assignment of interventions: blinding Who will be blinded {17a} The patients were not able to see the allocation, even though it is not possible to blind the rehabilitation trainers or assessors. Procedure for unblinding if needed {17b} N/A the emergency unblinding of the participants and rehabilitation trainers in our trial is irrelevant because it is impossible to blind them. Data collection and management Plans for assessment and collection of outcomes {18a} To ensure the quality of the research, we will conduct a thorough evaluation of the recruited doctors, rehabilitation therapists, assessors, and pertinent equipment prior to the commencement of the study. The following specific steps are taken: The experimental procedure was performed entirely by the recruited doctors. The therapists received instructions on the proper conduct of the training program and the management of potential adverse events that may arise during training. The assessors received training in the suitable handling and processing of outcome indicators. The lower limb rehabilitation robot (Novoskeleton AVIC Trands Robot, electromyography/evoked potential instrument NDI-096-C1) and electro-stimulator (Xiangyu Electrode Sheet Model 2.0 aperture (TENS)) were debugged to achieve the optimal running state of the equipment. Plans to promote participant retention and complete follow-up {18b} The subsequent evaluation was conducted 8 weeks after completing the training program. The participants were contacted via telephone and invited to the hospital to undergo the assessment. Data management {19} The hospital’s safety supervision committee oversees the project, which is tasked with evaluating experimental design, scientific rigor, participant safety, adherence to medical ethics, and proper data management. Strict measures were implemented to safeguard the privacy rights of each participant. Initial data and outcome indicators were securely stored in a highly protected database, and anonymization procedures were rigorously followed to ensure the safety and confidentiality of all participants. Confidentiality {27} Confidentiality rules were strictly followed during the experiment to gather, distribute, and safeguard personal information of potential and enrolled participants. Before starting the study, each participant provided informed consent, including a detailed explanation of the study’s aim, procedures, and potential hazards. The consent was obtained via a particular protocol code. Throughout the study, all the gathered data undergo confidentiality and was securely stored, with access limited exclusively to authorized individuals responsible for data analysis and trial supervision. Once the trial ended, personal information was protected, and any remaining identifiable data (specific protocol code) was securely stored for the necessary retention period. This was done in accordance with institutional and regulatory guidelines that ensure confidentiality and data protection. Plans for collection, laboratory evaluation, and storage of biological specimens for genetic or molecular analysis in this trial/future use {33} N/A. Biological specimens are not relevant to our trial. Statistical analysis {20a} Two separate researchers performed data entry to ensure that the accuracy of the input data can be verified. The data were analyzed via the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) version 26. Data distribution was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test and normal probability plots, and Levene’s test evaluated homogeneity of variances. Baseline group differences were analyzed using independent-samples t -tests (with Welch’s correction where variances were unequal) and χ 2 tests or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical data. A repeated-measures multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) was first conducted with time (baseline, 8 weeks) as the within-subject factor and group (RAGT + tSCS vs. CPT + tSCS) as the between-subject factor. The significant time × group multivariate effect (Pillai’s trace = 0.982, F (9, 10) = 59.946, p < 0.001) justified univariate follow-ups. For each outcome, Berg Balance Scale (BBS), Timed Up and Go (TUG), 10-m walk test (10MWT), Walking Index for Spinal Cord Injury II (WISCI-II), integrated EMG (iEMG), and ASIA motor score, a repeated-measures general linear model (GLM) was fitted with group as the between-subject factor and time as the within-subject factor. The group × time interaction was the primary test of treatment effect. As only two time points were analyzed, sphericity was not applicable, and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons were used for post hoc contrasts [ – ]. Discussion Principal findings This randomized trial tested whether pairing robot-assisted gait training (RAGT) with transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) confers greater benefit than an equally dosed program of conventional physical therapy (CPT) paired with the same tSCS protocol in people with incomplete, intermediate SCI. Groups were well matched at baseline on sex and all clinical and neurophysiological measures (all p ≥ 0.096), supporting unbiased estimation of treatment effects. Across 8 weeks, both arms improved substantially; however, improvement trajectories consistently favored RAGT + tSCS. Significant time × group interactions were observed for the Berg Balance Scale (BBS; F = 42.465, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.702), Timed Up and Go (TUG; F = 97.500, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.844), WISCI-II ( F = 8.528, p = 0.009, partial η 2 = 0.321), ASIA motor ( F = 56.639, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.759), and three of four intramuscular EMG (iEMG) targets: vastus lateralis, tibialis anterior, and gastrocnemius medialis (all p < 0.001; partial η 2 = 0.880, 0.859, 0.924, respectively). Post-intervention contrasts underscored clinically meaningful advantages: adjusted BBS was higher by + 7.67 points (95% CI, 5.14–10.19; partial η 2 = 0.708); TUG was faster by − 10.91 s, WISCI-II by + 1.26 points, and ASIA motor by + 7.93 points; and iEMG amplitudes were substantially larger in agonists critical for stance and foot-clearance (e.g., tibialis anterior + 217.7 µV). The 10-m walk test (10MWT) increased similarly in both groups (RAGT + tSCS + 0.092 m/s vs CPT + tSCS + 0.086 m/s, between-group p = 0.885), a pattern addressed below. How our findings fit with and extend current evidence Our result pattern mirrors high-quality syntheses of randomized trials comparing robotic exoskeleton gait training (REGT) with conventional therapy. A 2025 meta-analysis of 15 RCTs ( n = 579) found that, on average, REGT does not outperform conventional therapy for walking speed (10MWT weighted mean difference [WMD] − 0.03 m/s, p = 0.08) or 6-min walk distance (6MWT WMD − 1.83 m, p = 0.78) while consistently improving TUG (WMD 6.62 s, p = 0.04), WISCI-II (WMD 2.17, p = 0.0001), and lower-extremity motor scores (LEMS WMD 1.33, p = 0.0005) [ ]. Device family matters: in subgroup analyses, Lokomat improved WISCI-II (WMD 2.05, p = 0.005) and LEMS (WMD 1.22, p = 0.002), while wearable exoskeletons improved WISCI-II (WMD 2.75, p = 0.0005) but not LEMS (WMD 2.88, p = 0.06) [ , ]. Timing also moderates effects: within ≤ 6-month post-injury, REGT and conventional therapy are roughly equivalent for speed/distance, whereas beyond 6 months conventional therapy may hold an advantage for speed [ ]. These patterns, stronger effects on dynamic balance, ambulation complexity, and motor scores than on short-distance speed, map closely onto our between-group differences (BBS, TUG, WISCI-II, ASIA motor) and the non-separation on 10MWT at 8 weeks. Crucially, convergent evidence indicates that adding tSCS to standardized robotic stepping can unlock advantages that are not always seen with RAGT alone, particularly after a consolidation interval. In a double-blind, sham-controlled RCT pairing tSCS with a fixed Lokomat program ( n = 27), no between-group differences were evident immediately poststimulation block for primary outcomes; however, superiority of active tSCS emerged at 1-month follow-up for LEMS (Δ 3.3 points, p = 0.033), 10MWT (faster by 0.037 m/s, p = 0.030), TUG (− 4.7 s, p = 0.030), and WISCI-II (+ 3.4 points, p = 0.023). A larger proportion achieved 10-m walking (80% vs 73.9%, p = 0.019) [ – ]. Our 8-week post-intervention gains in balance, functional mobility, and ambulation level, paired with parallel 10MWT changes, are therefore consistent with a delayed-superiority pattern for speed that is expected to manifest after additional overground practice. Mechanistic interpretation: state-dependent neuromodulation during task-specific stepping tSCS likely acts as a neural gain controller, modulating posterior-root afferents and spinal interneuronal networks to raise state-dependent excitability during locomotor practice. When combined with the high-dose, proprioception-rich stepping and weight-bearing provided by RAGT, the intervention co-engages descending drive and spinal pattern-generating circuits under conditions that favor Hebbian plasticity and sensorimotor reweighting [ , ]. The strongest neuromechanical signals in our data, very large interactions for iEMG in tibialis anterior, vastus lateralis, and gastrocnemius medialis, map onto the biomechanical substrates of improved BBS

When combined with the high-dose, proprioception-rich stepping and weight-bearing provided by RAGT, the intervention co-engages descending drive and spinal pattern-generating circuits under conditions that favor Hebbian plasticity and sensorimotor reweighting [ , ]. The strongest neuromechanical signals in our data, very large interactions for iEMG in tibialis anterior, vastus lateralis, and gastrocnemius medialis, map onto the biomechanical substrates of improved BBS and faster TUG (ankle strategy, knee stabilization, push-off). The absence of a group interaction for biceps femoris is coherent with (i) the specific task demands emphasized by our progression and (ii) measurement selectivity: by using iEMG, which offers higher spatial specificity and signal-to-noise than surface EMG in neurological cohorts, we increase confidence that the observed changes reflect true neural recruitment rather than cross-talk or adiposity-related filtering [ , ]. Independent neurophysiology from the sham-controlled RCT, greater tibialis-anterior MEP amplitude with active tSCS, converges with our iEMG pattern and further supports a corticospinal/spinal priming mechanism that consolidates with subsequent conventional sessions [ , ]. Why did speed not separate at 8 weeks and why it might with consolidation Our nonsignificant between-group difference in 10MWT (− 0.002 m/s, p = 0.885) should be interpreted in context. First, treadmill-based RAGT emphasizes kinematic guidance, loading, and postural control, components that translate more directly to TUG/WISCI-II than to short distance, overground peak velocity unless explicit speed-targeted overground progression is incorporated [ , ]. Second, speed is notably sensitive to post-injury timing and dose; pooled RCT evidence indicates little to no advantage of REGT over conventional care for speed in the subacute window, with conventional care sometimes outperforming REGT > 6 months after injury [ , ]. Third, the double-blind tSCS + Lokomat RCT demonstrates that speed gains can lag, emerging after a month of continued practice (Δ 0.037 m/s) [ , ]. Finally, at the very low baseline velocities in our cohort (~ 0.23–0.24 m/s), absolute changes that are clinically meaningful may remain below between-group detectability in modest samples and with heterogeneous assistive-device use, one reason meta-analyses urge reporting of effect sizes and responder analyses, not just p -values [ , ]. Together, these considerations support a working model in which RAGT + tSCS first improves balance and complex mobility and primes the system for speed; differentiated 10MWT may then require targeted overground progression and a consolidation interval. Dose, progression, and mediators Training dose and progression likely contributed to the observed between-group differences. Body-weight support (BWS) requirements correlated strongly and negatively with assignment at session 1 ( r = − 0.886, p < 0.001) and session 20 ( r = − 0.867, p < 0.001), indicating more aggressive BWS reduction in the robotic arm, a plausible treatment mediator rather than a confound, because lowering support is intrinsic to the therapeutic mechanism that tSCS may help tolerate by increasing network excitability. Anthropometrics and time since injury showed expected collinearities (e.g., age with weight and height) but did not differ by group, reducing the likelihood of systematic confounding. These observations align with meta-analytic notes that dose heterogeneity (30–90 min per session, 4–8 weeks total) and device-specific progression strategies contribute to between-study dispersion of effect sizes [ , ]. Safety, feasibility, and broader health benefits Although our trial was not powered for safety endpoints, our experience accords with reports that pairing tSCS with stepping is generally well tolerated and free of serious adverse events when delivered under standard precautions [ ]. Across RAGT trials and syntheses, REGT is likewise framed as safe and feasible in both inpatient and outpatient settings, with favorable cardiovascular adaptations reported over extended programs. Of note, for clinical translation, randomized evidence suggests respiratory benefits with REGT (FEV1 WMD + 0.60 L, p = 0.03), even though effects on FVC and PEF are less consistent (two RCTs, n = 34) [ , ]. These secondary system outcomes, together with potential improvements in orthostatic tolerance and aerobic capacity reported in contemporary reviews, support earlier mobilization and may compound the functional gains of neuromodulation-augmented stepping [ , , ]. Strengths and limitations Our trial’s strengths include randomization, balanced baselines, a state-dependent design holding tSCS constant to isolate the incremental effect of high-dose robotic stepping, and triangulated endpoints (clinical, performance, muscle-specific iEMG) showing concordant effects across repeated-measures GLM and baseline-adjusted ANCOVA (e.g., BBS adjusted + 7.67). Methodological work shows that in randomized pre- and post-designs, ANCOVA (post adjusted for baseline) provides greater power and precision than change scores or multiple t -tests by reducing residual variance and addressing residual baseline differences [ – ]. Strengths and limitations Our trial’s strengths include randomization, balanced baselines, a state-dependent design holding tSCS constant to isolate the incremental effect of high-dose robotic stepping, and triangulated endpoints (clinical, performance, muscle-specific iEMG) showing concordant effects across repeated-measures GLM and baseline-adjusted ANCOVA (e.g., BBS adjusted + 7.67). Methodological work shows that in randomized pre- and post-designs, ANCOVA (post adjusted for baseline) provides greater power and precision than change scores or multiple t -tests by reducing residual variance and addressing residual baseline differences [ – ]. Limitations include modest sample size (particularly for velocity outcomes with floor effects), the absence of a post-block follow-up (precluding direct observation of delayed superiority for speed), and device or contextual specificity (treadmill-based RAGT with specific progression heuristics), which may limit generalizability across the broader RAGT ecosystem [ , ]. As emphasized by recent syntheses, heterogeneity in dose, device, chronicity, and inclusion of some AIS-A participants can blunt pooled speed effects and warrant careful reporting of effect sizes, precision, and responders alongside null hypothesis tests [ , ]. These constraints also justify the use of multivariate and repeated-measures models rather than the initially planned t -tests, providing a more efficient and statistically stable framework that allowed correlated endpoints to be analyzed jointly, controlled type 1 error, and preserved power despite the limited sample size and inter-outcome covariance [ , ]. Clinical implications and future directions For people with incomplete SCI, these results support integrating tSCS during high-dose robotic stepping to accelerate gains in balance, complex mobility, ambulation level, and motor index, domains with clear relevance toward safety, transfers, turning, and discharge independence. To realize durable advantages in speed, programs should add explicit, overground, speed-targeted progression and schedule follow-up assessments to capture neuromodulation-enabled consolidation. Future trials should (i) standardize BWS and speed-progression algorithms, (ii) compare device families head-to-head under identical neuromodulation, (iii) leverage biomarkers (baseline corticospinal excitability, iEMG motor-unit metrics) to profile responders, and (iv) extend observation windows beyond the intervention block to adjudicate the priming-and-consolidation hypothesis more directly [ , , , , ]. Given preliminary signals for cardiorespiratory benefits, incorporating spirometry and ambulatory hemodynamics could clarify secondary health impacts that matter for real-world participation [ , , ]. Conclusions RAGT paired with tSCS produced larger improvements than CPT + tSCS in balance (BBS), functional mobility (TUG), ambulation level (WISCI-II), ASIA motor, and targeted muscle recruitment (iEMG), with parallel changes in short-distance walking speed at 8 weeks. Read against current evidence, the data support a model in which tSCS gates spinal networks during task-specific stepping to amplify the domains RAGT already tends to improve, while speed differentials are expected to emerge with consolidation and speed-focused overground practice. This neuromodulation-augmented approach is biologically plausible, clinically feasible, and aligned with evolving RCT syntheses; it merits scaled testing with device-specific optimization, longer follow-up, and responder-oriented design.
